profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This Flexential cluster spans Georgia (Alpharetta, Douglasville, Norcross), Florida (Fort Lauderdale, Jacksonville, Tampa), North Carolina (Charlotte, Morrisville), and Tennessee (Brentwood, Franklin), the historic Southeastern United States footprint of Peak 10. According to Flexential own company history page, Peak 10 was founded in 2000 and built a strong regional presence across the Southeastern US. In 2017 Peak 10 purchased ViaWest, merging the two regionally dominant data center providers, and the combined company rebranded as Flexential in 2018. Flexential also acquired AppliedTrust and INetU in 2015 to expand its professional services and cloud offerings. Flexential operates 40 plus data centers across 18 national markets under CEO Ryan Mallory. No building specific address or individual MW figures for these particular registry rows were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
At 6 MW of published IT capacity across 142,475 square feet of technical space, this campus is a mid-size colocation facility. At 10 kW per rack, a common enterprise colocation density, 6 MW supports roughly 600 racks; at 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, the same load supports roughly 150 racks. The published figure is IT load, not gross building power, so power usage effectiveness overhead is not captured in the 6 MW number. No redundancy tier or cooling architecture is published on the operator's spec page.

The six certifications qualify this campus to host regulated workloads: SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 cover financial and operational controls audited over time, PCI DSS covers payment card data environments, HIPAA covers protected health information, ISO 27001 covers an audited information security management system, and SSAE 18 is the attestation standard underlying the SOC reports. Taken together, the certifications signal a compliance posture suited to enterprise and regulated-industry tenants. Which tenants are actually present is not published.

Among the 33 facilities this site has mapped in Georgia, only 2 have published a megawatt figure, and those two sum to 42 MW. This campus, at 6 MW, ranks second among the two with published figures, representing roughly 14 percent of the state's published IT capacity on this site. That share reflects data scarcity as much as market position: 31 of the 33 mapped Georgia facilities publish no MW figure, so the ranking describes what is visible to this site, not the full Georgia market.
